current_episode.title: Inside buildingSMART - The Future of IFC with Eric Bugeja

guest.titre: Chairperson, buildingSMART Australasia; Director, buildingSMART International
guest.bio_context: Eric Bugeja started his career as a mechanical engineer, initially working in a two-man company with a highly experienced Dutch engineer in his 60s who gave him complete flexibility to explore new technologies — an unusually formative experience for a graduate. He later moved through manufacturing automation and food processing consultancy before transitioning into BIM leadership roles at large design and construction firms, where he developed digital strategy and drove structured data adoption. He now runs his own consulting and training business, Kefron, while serving voluntarily as Chairperson of buildingSMART Australasia and Director of buildingSMART International, focusing on open standards, technology adoption, and digital engineering advocacy globally.

pending_qa.q: What are the risks of vendor lock-in for engineering firms and asset owners, and how do open standards help?
pending_qa.r: If one or two software vendors become dominant and an organisation's data is locked into their proprietary format, that organisation faces serious risk if the vendor goes bankrupt, discontinues the software, or raises prices arbitrarily due to a monopoly position. Open standards like IFC ensure that data remains accessible regardless of the software used — for example, an IFC file could still be opened 30 years from now without requiring a specific software version. This creates a competitive and resilient environment for both practitioners and software providers.

pending_qa.q: What are the most common mistakes organisations make when using IFC files, and how should they be used correctly?
pending_qa.r: A common mistake is that designers simply export an IFC file with no specific instructions, resulting in massive, unmanageable files containing every attribute and geometry element whether needed or not. The correct approach is for clients to specify exactly what parameters and level of detail are required from the IFC export — for instance, stating which attributes are needed and how the export should be configured — so the file serves a defined purpose. The frustration in the industry largely stems from a lack of education on the limitations of IFC from both a geometry and data perspective.

pending_qa.q: What is the future direction of IFC and open standards — are we moving beyond file-based data exchange?
pending_qa.r: buildingSMART is actively working on the next generation of open standards that moves away from file-based, fixed packets of information toward cloud-based, AI-capable, modularised, and connected data environments. In this future model, a design model, an asset register, and a GIS system would not be three separate things requiring reconciliation, but rather three views of the same underlying dataset, accessible via APIs and connected systems. File-based transmission will continue for some time, but the direction is clearly toward information being accessed rather than sent.

pending_qa.q: How does structured data from open standards like IFC improve AI outcomes in construction?
pending_qa.r: AI systems are only as good as the data they are trained on, so fragmented, inconsistent, and ungoverned information environments do not get solved by AI — they get scaled by it, making it harder to recover. Conversely, when the industry uses structured data and consistent classification frameworks like IFC, AI has a reliable basis to produce genuinely useful results — for example, it can correctly identify that a model element is a door or a window because the schema defines it explicitly. Eric Bugeja notes that the construction industry's longstanding work on structured data, governed workflows, and classification actually puts it in a stronger position than many other sectors when it comes to leveraging AI effectively.

pending_qa.q: What is the governance and volunteer structure of buildingSMART, and how do working groups function?
pending_qa.r: The vast majority of people working within the buildingSMART community do so on a voluntary basis, including Eric Bugeja himself in his roles as Chairperson and Director. Working groups — for example in linear infrastructure and airports — bring together government bodies, vendors, designers, and universities to solve problems, share best practices around open standards, and feed back unmet requirements to buildingSMART International so the standards can evolve. buildingSMART Australasia recently held its annual exchange conference in Brisbane, with additional regional events planned including one in New Zealand later in the year.

pending_qa.q: What is Eric Bugeja's view on AI and its implications for the construction industry — threat or opportunity?
pending_qa.r: Eric Bugeja frames AI not as a Terminator-style existential threat but as a powerful tool whose value is entirely dependent on the quality and structure of the underlying data it uses. He acknowledges that even as a long-time technology enthusiast, the current capabilities of AI are surprising to him, but stresses that the construction industry's historical underreporting of project failures means AI trained on incomplete historical data risks repeating poor decisions — for instance, reusing a construction programme that appeared successful on paper but was never updated with what actually happened. The industry's structured data frameworks, if properly implemented, represent a significant competitive advantage in the AI era.
